description: If Earth Could Sing is an interactive Earth data jukebox. Visitors explore a 3D globe, choose a destination, and hear NASA temperature, precipitation, and wind data translated into music. A global exhibit also turns NASA temperature maps from 1881 to 2023 into sound. Visitors can inspect how each sound relates to the data and compare places or time periods. The project offers another way to explore climate patterns through listening alongside maps and numbers. Solo team project.
summary: If Earth Could Sing is an interactive Earth data jukebox that turns NASA climate and weather data into music. Visitors explore a 3D globe and listen to patterns in the Amazon, Himalayas, Sahara, and Greenland. Temperature shapes the melody, precipitation sets rhythmic activity, and wind adds texture. Visitors can compare places and time periods, then inspect the numbers and rules behind each sound. A global exhibit pairs NASA temperature maps from 1881–2023 with music driven by GISTEMP temperature anomalies and patterns extracted from the images. The project addresses the Earth Information Jukebox challenge by making NASA data something people can explore through listening as well as looking. It offers an engaging entry point for people unfamiliar with climate charts, while keeping source information, uncertainty, and the distinction between data and musical interpretation visible.
details:
If Earth Could Sing is an interactive website that turns NASA Earth data into music. Built for the Earth Information Jukebox challenge, it lets visitors explore climate patterns through sound, maps, photographs, and numbers.

Visitors begin with a 3D globe and choose one of four destinations: the Amazon Rainforest, the Himalayas, the Sahara, or the Greenland Ice Sheet. Each destination combines NASA imagery with temperature, precipitation, and wind data from a specific NASA POWER sampling point. Additional destinations are marked “Coming soon” and do not yet provide data or audio.

How the data becomes music:

The music is generated during playback. Temperature controls melody pitch, precipitation controls the number of rhythmic notes, and wind controls the intensity and brightness of a sound texture. These relationships follow explicit, reproducible rules. Each destination uses the same mapping scale within a listening mode, allowing visitors to compare places consistently.

Three sound palettes offer different listening experiences: Floating, Jazz trio, and Original synth. Visitors can isolate individual data layers, adjust playback speed, or move through the timeline. Optional accompaniment is labeled separately and can be muted because it carries no data.

The Decode panel explains the selected step, showing its original values and how they translate into sound. This makes the musical choices visible rather than asking visitors to interpret the audio without context.

Exploring seasons and change:

Climate portrait mode plays twelve months of average conditions at a sampling point. It highlights seasonal differences, such as the Himalayan monsoon or Greenland’s long, cold winter.

Change over time mode presents annual anomalies relative to each point’s own 1991–2020 baseline. Visitors can also compare two decades at one location or two locations during the same period, then reveal charts and numerical differences alongside what they heard.

The Earth Information Center exhibit:

A separate exhibit uses 143 annual frames from NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio temperature visualization, covering 1881–2023. The website analyzes map colors to shape musical layers, including a sequence that scans from southern to northern latitudes.

Calibrated global annual temperature anomalies from NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 control the main melody. The exhibit distinguishes these numerical measurements from the relative color information extracted from the images. Its timeline connects the changing map, displayed year, values, and generated sound.

Purpose and limitations:

The project gives visitors another way to notice and explore patterns in Earth data. A listener can hear a seasonal rhythm or a shift in pitch, then inspect the values behind it. It is intended for public exploration and educational demonstrations.

The sounds are designed translations, not recordings of Earth. NASA POWER weather values come from model and reanalysis products, and each destination represents one grid cell rather than an entire region. The global visualization uses running averages that differ from calendar-year GISTEMP values. Comparisons include uncertainty and natural variability and do not establish the cause of a change.

The website was developed with React, TypeScript, and Vite. Claude Code assisted with development, refinement, testing support, and documentation. NASA data and imagery are credited in the website’s Sources section.
